q: 2-opt move for the TSP: what is exchanged, how many moves are there, and what is the constant-time gain test?
a:
Remove the tour edges $\{\pi_i,\pi_{i+1}\}$ and $\{\pi_j,\pi_{j+1}\}$ and add $\{\pi_i,\pi_j\}$ and $\{\pi_{i+1},\pi_{j+1}\}$; the path between $\pi_{i+1}$ and $\pi_j$ is reversed. There are $O(n^2)$ possible exchanges.
Gain test in $O(1)$: $\Delta_{ij}=d(\pi_i,\pi_j)+d(\pi_{i+1},\pi_{j+1})-d(\pi_i,\pi_{i+1})-d(\pi_j,\pi_{j+1})$; the move improves the tour iff $\Delta_{ij} \lt 0$.

source.label: DM841 Discrete Optimization — Heuristics: Local Search for the Traveling Salesman Problem (M. Chiarandini, SDU, slides)

q: Symmetric TSP tour 1-2-3-4-5-1 with $d(1,2)=4$, $d(3,4)=6$, $d(1,3)=3$, $d(2,4)=5$. A 2-opt move replaces the edges $\{1,2\}$ and $\{3,4\}$ by $\{1,3\}$ and $\{2,4\}$. What is the change $\Delta$ in tour length?
explain: $\Delta=d(1,3)+d(2,4)-d(1,2)-d(3,4)=3+5-4-6=-2 \lt 0$: the move is improving. Only the four exchanged edges matter, which is why the evaluation takes constant time.

source.label: DM841 Discrete Optimization — Heuristics: Local Search for the Traveling Salesman Problem (M. Chiarandini, SDU, slides)

q: Tour 1-2-3-4-5-1. A 2-opt move removes the edges $\{1,2\}$ and $\{3,4\}$ and adds $\{1,3\}$ and $\{2,4\}$. What is the resulting tour?
explain: The segment between the two removed edges (cities 2, 3) is reversed: 1-3-2-4-5-1, which uses the new edges $\{1,3\}$ and $\{2,4\}$ and keeps $\{2,3\}$, $\{4,5\}$, $\{5,1\}$. The other options still contain a removed edge or use edges that were not added.

source.label: DM841 Discrete Optimization — Heuristics: Local Search for the Traveling Salesman Problem (M. Chiarandini, SDU, slides)

q: TSP neighbourhoods beyond 2-opt: describe 3-opt and Or-opt and give the number of exchanges of each.
a:
3-opt: remove three edges and reconnect the three paths; $O(n^3)$ exchanges; sub-paths may be reversed.
Or-opt: relocate a chain of one, two or three consecutive vertices between two other vertices; $O(n^2)$ exchanges and no reversal of sub-paths (so it is also usable for asymmetric problems).
A local-search step costs: neighbourhood size, move evaluation (delta evaluation), executing the move, updating auxiliary data. Typical speed-ups: neighbour (candidate) lists, fixed-radius search, don't-look bits.

source.label: DM841 Discrete Optimization — Heuristics: Local Search for the Traveling Salesman Problem (M. Chiarandini, SDU, slides)

q: In first-improvement 2-opt local search for the TSP, a single scan over all pairs $(i,j)$ in which every improving move encountered is applied guarantees that the final tour is locally optimal for the 2-exchange neighbourhood.
explain: After a move has been applied, pairs that were already examined may have become improving. The scan must be repeated until a complete pass finds no improving move; only then is the tour a local optimum of the 2-exchange neighbourhood.

source.label: DM841 Discrete Optimization — Heuristics: Local Search for the Traveling Salesman Problem (M. Chiarandini, SDU, slides)

q: For a TSP tour on $n=10$ cities, how many neighbouring tours does the 2-opt neighbourhood contain? (Use the count $n(n-3)/2$.)
explain: A 2-opt move is determined by two non-adjacent tour edges: $n(n-3)/2=10\cdot 7/2=35$. Each neighbour is evaluated in $O(1)$ because only four edge costs change; a naive $k$-opt iteration costs $O(n^k)$. Without special problem structure, local search gives no guarantee on the distance to the global optimum.

source.label: "Local Search with Two-Opt" (MIT 15.DOTs wiki page on a TSP project)

q: What is a metaheuristic, and why is plain hill climbing (iterative improvement) not enough?
a:
A metaheuristic is a generic strategy that guides an underlying problem-specific heuristic (e.g. a local search) in order to improve its performance or robustness.
Hill climbing stops at the first local optimum of its neighbourhood, often quickly. Random restart is the simplest escape, but it throws away the whole search history; simulated annealing, tabu search, iterated local search and evolutionary methods are more refined ways of escaping local optima.

source.label: CS4234 Optimisation Algorithms, Lecture 10 — Meta-heuristics (S. Gilbert / S. Halim, National University of Singapore; based on Hoos & Stützle's SLS book slides)

q: Simulated annealing for a minimisation problem with the Metropolis rule: a neighbour $s'$ that is worse than the current solution $s$ is accepted with probability $\exp((f(s)-f(s'))/T)$. The current tour has length 100 and the proposed neighbour has length 104. What is the acceptance probability at temperature $T=10$?
explain: $\exp((100-104)/10)=e^{-0.4}\approx 0.670$. At $T=1$ the same move would be accepted with probability $e^{-4}\approx 0.018$: a high temperature makes the search close to a random walk, a low temperature close to pure descent.

source.label: CS4234 Optimisation Algorithms, Lecture 10 — Meta-heuristics (S. Gilbert / S. Halim, National University of Singapore; based on Hoos & Stützle's SLS book slides)

q: Simulated annealing: state the acceptance rule and the components of an annealing (cooling) schedule.
a:
Pick a neighbour $s'$ of $s$ at random; accept it with probability 1 if $f(s')\le f(s)$, otherwise with probability $\exp((f(s)-f(s'))/T)$ (minimisation). The temperature $T$ controls how likely worsening moves are.
Cooling schedule: initial temperature $T_0$; update rule (e.g. geometric cooling $T:=\alpha T$); number of steps per temperature (often a multiple of the neighbourhood size); termination (often based on the acceptance ratio).
Convergence to an optimum is only guaranteed under extremely slow cooling, a result of little practical relevance; in practice the aim is to find good solutions quickly.

source.label: CS4234 Optimisation Algorithms, Lecture 10 — Meta-heuristics (S. Gilbert / S. Halim, National University of Singapore; based on Hoos & Stützle's SLS book slides)

q: Tabu search: how does it escape local minima? Define tabu tenure and aspiration criterion.
a:
Tabu search uses memory. After each step the solution components just added or removed are declared tabu for a fixed number of steps, the tabu tenure; the search moves to the best admissible (non-tabu) neighbour even if it is worse than the current solution.
An aspiration criterion overrides the tabu status, typically when the move leads to a new best solution.
Longer-term memory supports intensification (return to elite solutions, freeze components) and diversification (force rarely used components).

source.label: CS4234 Optimisation Algorithms, Lecture 10 — Meta-heuristics (S. Gilbert / S. Halim, National University of Singapore; based on Hoos & Stützle's SLS book slides)

q: In tabu search, what is the typical effect of choosing the tabu tenure too small?
options: Too few neighbours remain admissible, so the search becomes ineffective.
The aspiration criterion can no longer be triggered.
The method degenerates into random restart.
The search cycles or stagnates around the same local minimum.
explain: With a short tenure, recently reversed moves quickly become admissible again and the search falls back into the local minimum it just left (cycling). A tenure that is too large has the opposite problem: too few admissible neighbours. Robust tabu search draws the tenure at random from an interval; reactive tabu search adapts it during the run.

source.label: CS4234 Optimisation Algorithms, Lecture 10 — Meta-heuristics (S. Gilbert / S. Halim, National University of Singapore; based on Hoos & Stützle's SLS book slides)

q: Iterated local search (ILS): what are its components, and how strong should the perturbation be?
a:
ILS alternates a subsidiary local search (intensification, ends in a local optimum) with a perturbation (diversification) and an acceptance criterion; the search is a walk in the space of local optima.
The perturbation must not be easily undone by the local search: for the TSP with 2-opt, the 'double-bridge' 4-exchange move. Too weak: the search falls back into the same local optimum. Too strong: it behaves like random restart.

source.label: CS4234 Optimisation Algorithms, Lecture 10 — Meta-heuristics (S. Gilbert / S. Halim, National University of Singapore; based on Hoos & Stützle's SLS book slides)

q: Evolutionary / genetic algorithms: name the three operators applied to the population. What is a memetic algorithm?
a:
A population of solutions is maintained and iterated through recombination (build offspring from fragments of parents), mutation (small random changes, controlled by a mutation rate) and selection (fitter solutions survive with higher probability, e.g. roulette-wheel selection; elitist strategies always keep the best).
A memetic algorithm is a genetic algorithm plus local search applied to the offspring, because pure genetic algorithms lack intensification.

source.label: CS4234 Optimisation Algorithms, Lecture 10 — Meta-heuristics (S. Gilbert / S. Halim, National University of Singapore; based on Hoos & Stützle's SLS book slides)

q: Variable neighbourhood search: which observations is it based on, and how do variable neighbourhood descent (VND) and basic VNS work?
a:
Observations: a local minimum for one neighbourhood is not necessarily a local minimum for another; a global optimum is locally optimal for all neighbourhoods. So change the neighbourhood systematically, using $N_1,\dots,N_{k_{\max}}$ (typically ordered from smallest to largest).
VND: $k\leftarrow 1$; repeat: $s'\leftarrow$ best neighbour of $s$ in $N_k$; if $f(s') \lt f(s)$ then $s\leftarrow s'$, $k\leftarrow 1$, else $k\leftarrow k+1$; until $k=k_{\max}$. The result is locally optimal for all the neighbourhoods.
Basic VNS: the best-neighbour step is replaced by 'shaking' ($s'\leftarrow$ a random solution in $N_k(s)$) followed by a local search from $s'$ giving $s''$; accept and reset $k\leftarrow 1$ if $f(s'') \lt f(s)$, otherwise $k\leftarrow k+1$.

source.label: DM841 Discrete Optimization, Lecture 8 — Stochastic Local Search and Metaheuristics (M. Chiarandini, SDU)

q: Constructive heuristics for the TSP: describe nearest neighbour, greedy edge selection and insertion heuristics (cheapest / farthest insertion).
a:
Nearest neighbour: from the current vertex go to the cheapest unvisited vertex; $O(n^2)$; tends to finish with a few very expensive edges.
Greedy edge selection: sort the edges by cost and add each one unless it creates a vertex of degree 3 or a cycle shorter than $n$; $O(n^2\log n)$.
Insertion: start from a small subtour and insert the remaining vertices one by one. Cheapest insertion picks the vertex and position with the smallest increase in length; farthest insertion inserts the vertex whose minimum distance to the subtour is largest (it fixes the overall shape of the tour early).

source.label: Mathematics of Operational Research notes, section 14 "Heuristic Algorithms" (F. Fischer, Queen Mary University of London)

q: Asymmetric TSP on 5 cities with cost matrix (row = from, column = to) $$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0&4&4\\4&0&1&0&4\\4&4&0&1&0\\0&4&4&0&1\\1&0&4&4&0\end{pmatrix}.$$ (a) Compute the cost of the tour 1→2→3→4→5→1. (b) Compute the costs of the neighbouring tours 1→3→2→4→5→1, 1→2→4→3→5→1 and 1→2→3→5→4→1 (two consecutive cities exchanged). (c) Compute the cost of the tour 1→3→5→2→4→1. What does this example show about local search?
model:
(a) $a_{12}+a_{23}+a_{34}+a_{45}+a_{51}=1+1+1+1+1=5$.
(b) $c(13245)=a_{13}+a_{32}+a_{24}+a_{45}+a_{51}=0+4+0+1+1=6$; $c(12435)=1+0+4+0+1=6$; $c(12354)=1+1+0+4+0=6$. All are worse than 5 (in fact every 2-OPT neighbour of 12345 is worse), so 12345 is a local optimum.
(c) $c(13524)=a_{13}+a_{35}+a_{52}+a_{24}+a_{41}=0$: the global optimum. Local search can stop at a local optimum (cost 5) that is not globally optimal (cost 0); without special structure it gives no guarantee.
rubric: Conclusion: a 2-OPT local optimum need not be a global optimum

source.label: Mathematics of Operational Research notes, section 14 "Heuristic Algorithms" (F. Fischer, Queen Mary University of London)

q: Symmetric TSP on 4 cities with $w(1,2)=25$, $w(1,3)=30$, $w(1,4)=20$, $w(2,3)=35$, $w(2,4)=10$, $w(3,4)=15$. What is the length of the tour built by the nearest-neighbour heuristic started at city 1?
explain: $1\to 4$ (20), then the nearest unvisited city from 4 is 2 (10), then 3 (35), and back to 1 (30): $20+10+35+30=95$. The optimal tour 1-2-4-3-1 has length $25+10+15+30=80$, so nearest neighbour is $15/80=18.75\%$ above the optimum: the last edges are expensive.

source.label: CIS 189 Lecture 11 — TSP Techniques (R. Menezes, University of Pennsylvania, slides)

q: Symmetric TSP on 4 cities with $w(1,2)=25$, $w(1,3)=30$, $w(1,4)=20$, $w(2,3)=35$, $w(2,4)=10$, $w(3,4)=15$. Run the nearest insertion heuristic from city 1: repeatedly take the city not yet in the subtour that is closest to the subtour and insert it between the pair of consecutive subtour cities $t_i,t_{i+1}$ that minimises $w(t_i,v)+w(v,t_{i+1})-w(t_i,t_{i+1})$. Give the successive subtours, the insertion costs and the length of the final tour.
model:
Start with $\{1\}$; the nearest city is 4: subtour 1-4-1 of length 40.
City closest to the subtour: 2 (distance 10 from city 4; city 3 is at distance 15). Insertion cost $25+10-20=15$ at either position: subtour 1-2-4-1 of length 55.
Insert 3: between 1 and 2: $30+35-25=40$; between 2 and 4: $35+15-10=40$; between 4 and 1: $15+30-20=25$. Final tour 1-2-4-3-1 of length $55+25=80$, which is optimal.
rubric: City 2 inserted next with cost 15, subtour length 55

q: Symmetric TSP on 4 cities with $w(1,2)=25$, $w(1,3)=30$, $w(1,4)=20$, $w(2,3)=35$, $w(2,4)=10$, $w(3,4)=15$. Farthest insertion from city 1 starts with the subtour 1-3-1 (city 3 is farthest from city 1). Which city is inserted next, and what is the length of the final tour (each city is inserted at its cheapest position)?
options: City 4, because it is closest to the subtour; final length 80
City 2, because its distance to the subtour ($\min\{25,35\}=25$) exceeds that of city 4 ($\min\{20,15\}=15$); final tour 1-2-4-3-1 of length 80
City 2; final tour 1-2-3-4-1 of length 95
City 4; final length 95
explain: Farthest insertion picks the city whose minimum distance to the subtour is largest: city 2 (25) rather than city 4 (15). Inserting 2 costs $25+35-30=30$: subtour 1-2-3-1 of length 90. City 4 is then inserted at the cheapest position: between 1 and 2: $20+10-25=5$; between 2 and 3: $10+15-35=-10$; between 3 and 1: $15+20-30=5$. Final tour 1-2-4-3-1 of length 80 (optimal).

source.label: CIS 189 Lecture 11 — TSP Techniques (R. Menezes, University of Pennsylvania, slides)

q: Symmetric TSP on 4 cities with $w(1,2)=25$, $w(1,3)=30$, $w(1,4)=20$, $w(2,3)=35$, $w(2,4)=10$, $w(3,4)=15$. Apply the Clarke-Wright savings heuristic with centre city 1: give the initial solution, the savings and the merges, and the final tour.
model:
Initial solution: the out-and-back tours 1-2-1, 1-3-1, 1-4-1 with total length $2(25+30+20)=150$.
Savings $s(i,j)=w(i,1)+w(1,j)-w(i,j)$: $s(2,3)=25+30-35=20$, $s(2,4)=25+20-10=35$, $s(3,4)=30+20-15=35$.
Process by decreasing saving: merge on (3,4): length $150-35=115$ (tour 1-3-4-1 and tour 1-2-1); merge on (2,4): length $115-35=80$. Final tour 1-2-4-3-1 of length 80, which is optimal (taking the two savings of 35 in the other order gives the same tour).

source.label: CIS 189 Lecture 11 — TSP Techniques (R. Menezes, University of Pennsylvania, slides)

q: State the Clarke-Wright savings heuristic. For which problem was it designed?
a:
Choose a centre $x$ and start from the $n-1$ out-and-back tours $x$-$v$-$x$. Compute the savings $s(i,j)=w(i,x)+w(x,j)-w(i,j)$ and process the pairs $(i,j)$ by decreasing saving: merge the two tours if $(i,x)$ and $(x,j)$ are still tour edges and $i$, $j$ are in different tours.
It was designed for vehicle routing ($x$ = depot), where a merge is skipped if it violates capacity or route-length limits.

source.label: CIS 189 Lecture 11 — TSP Techniques (R. Menezes, University of Pennsylvania, slides)

q: GRASP: what does one iteration consist of, and how is the restricted candidate list (RCL) built in the construction phase?
a:
GRASP (greedy randomized adaptive search procedure) is a multi-start method. Each iteration: (1) greedy randomized construction of a feasible solution, (2) local search from it to a local minimum. The best solution over all iterations is kept.
Construction: until the solution is complete, evaluate the incremental cost $c(e)$ of every candidate element; build $RCL=\{e: c(e)\le c_{\min}+\alpha(c_{\max}-c_{\min})\}$ (value-based; alternatively the $p$ best elements); pick an element of the RCL at random; add it; re-evaluate the incremental costs.
Greedy: the RCL only holds good elements. Randomized: random pick. Adaptive: costs are updated after each addition. For minimisation $\alpha=0$ is pure greedy and $\alpha=1$ purely random.

source.label: Greedy Randomized Adaptive Search Procedures (M. G. C. Resende, C. C. Ribeiro; chapter for the Handbook of Metaheuristics, author-hosted PDF)

q: GRASP construction step (minimisation) with the value-based restricted candidate list $RCL=\{e:\ c(e)\le c_{\min}+\alpha(c_{\max}-c_{\min})\}$. The candidate incremental costs are 4, 6, 7, 10, 12. Which candidates are in the RCL for $\alpha=0.25$?
explain: Threshold $=4+0.25\,(12-4)=6$, so the RCL contains the candidates with cost at most 6: $\{4,6\}$. For $\alpha=0$ the threshold is 4 (pure greedy, RCL $=\{4\}$); for $\alpha=1$ it is 12 (all five candidates, purely random construction).

source.label: Greedy Randomized Adaptive Search Procedures (M. G. C. Resende, C. C. Ribeiro; chapter for the Handbook of Metaheuristics, author-hosted PDF)

q: In the minimisation form of GRASP with $RCL=\{e:\ c(e)\le c_{\min}+\alpha(c_{\max}-c_{\min})\}$, the value $\alpha=1$ gives the pure greedy construction and $\alpha=0$ a purely random construction.
explain: It is the other way round: $\alpha=0$ keeps only the candidates of minimum incremental cost (pure greedy), while $\alpha=1$ admits every candidate (purely random). A larger RCL gives more diverse solutions with a worse average value, but after local search the best solution found is often better than the greedy one.

q: LP-rounding heuristic for minimum vertex cover (threshold rounding): what is the rule, why is the rounded solution feasible, and how do its value and the LP value bound the optimum?
a:
Solve the LP relaxation $\min\ \sum_i x_i$ s.t. $x_i+x_j\ge 1$ for every edge $\{i,j\}$, $0\le x\le 1$; its value is a lower (dual) bound on the optimum.
Rounding: take $S=\{i: x_i\ge 1/2\}$. $S$ is a cover, because each edge has an endpoint with value at least $1/2$. Its size is an upper (primal) bound, and $|S|\le 2\sum_i x_i=2\,z_{LP}\le 2\,z^*$.

source.label: COS 521 lecture slides "Using LP rounding to design approximation algorithms" (S. Arora, Princeton, 2005)

q: Minimum vertex cover on the triangle with vertices 1, 2, 3 (IP: $\min\ x_1+x_2+x_3$, $x_i+x_j\ge 1$ for each edge, $x$ binary). The LP relaxation returns $x=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$. What does threshold rounding (select vertex $i$ when $x_i\ge 1/2$) give, compared with the LP bound and the integer optimum?
options: A cover of size 2; LP bound 1.5; optimum 2
A cover of size 3; LP bound 2; optimum 3
An infeasible set of size 1; LP bound 1.5; optimum 2
A cover of size 3; LP bound 1.5; optimum 2
explain: All three vertices have $x_i=1/2$ and are selected: a feasible cover of size 3. The LP value is $1.5$ (dual bound) and the integer optimum is 2 (any two vertices). So $1.5\le 2\le 3$ and $3\le 2\times 1.5$: rounding gives a feasible solution (primal bound) that need not be optimal.

source.label: COS 521 lecture slides "Using LP rounding to design approximation algorithms" (S. Arora, Princeton, 2005)

q: A JuMP model has two integer variables $x$ and $y$, each with bounds $0\le\cdot\le 2.5$, and the objective $\max\ y$. A lazy-constraint callback adds $y-x\le 1$ whenever the callback point violates it, and $y+x\le 3$ whenever that one is violated. Which optimal solution does the solver return?
explain: Integrality and the bound 2.5 give $y\le 2$. With $y=2$, the lazy constraint $y-x\le 1$ forces $x\ge 1$ and $y+x\le 3$ forces $x\le 1$, so $(x,y)=(1,2)$. The points $(0,2)$ and $(2,2)$ each violate one lazy constraint and are rejected in the callback; $(0.5,2.5)$ is not integer.

source.label: JuMP tutorial — Callbacks

q: JuMP solver-independent callbacks: how are a user cut and a heuristic solution submitted in the JuMP callbacks tutorial, and which precaution is recommended when testing callbacks?
a:
User cut: separate a violated inequality from the fractional callback solution and submit it with MOI.UserCut(cb_data) (tutorial example: a 30-item knapsack with capacity 10).
Heuristic solution: build a candidate, e.g. floor.(x_vals), and submit it with MOI.HeuristicSolution(cb_data); the returned status says whether it was HEURISTIC_SOLUTION_ACCEPTED or rejected.
Precaution: where necessary turn off the solver's own cuts, heuristics and presolve, otherwise the solver may solve the model before ever calling your callback.

source.label: JuMP tutorial — Callbacks

q: Gurobi-specific callback written in Julia/JuMP: which calls and which parameter are needed?
a:
• Query callback information with Gurobi.GRBcbget.
  • Check GRB_CB_MIPNODE_STATUS before reading a node relaxation.
  • Call Gurobi.load_callback_variable_primal(cb_data, cb_where) before callback_value.
  • Set the parameter "LazyConstraints" to 1 if lazy constraints are submitted.
  • Stop the solve with Gurobi.GRBterminate; the termination status is then MOI.INTERRUPTED.

q: JuMP warm starts: which functions set primal and dual start values, and why does the tutorial first store the current solution in dictionaries?
a:
set_start_value(x, v) sets a primal start for a variable (or the primal value of a constraint) and set_dual_start_value(con, v) a dual start.
The tutorial's helper first caches value / dual of everything and only then calls the setters, because JuMP does not allow solution queries to be interleaved with model modifications. Not every solver accepts every kind of start; unsupported ones raise MOI.UnsupportedAttribute.

q: A MIP contains the constraint $x_1+x_2+x_3\ge 15$ and the variable bounds $x_1\le 7$, $x_2\le 3$, $x_3\le 5$. What can presolve conclude from this row alone?
options: $x_1=7$, $x_2=3$, $x_3=5$: the variables are fixed and can be removed from the model.
The constraint is redundant and can be deleted.
The model is infeasible.
Nothing; the LP relaxation has to be solved first.
explain: The largest possible left-hand side is $7+3+5=15$, so the constraint can only hold if every variable is at its upper bound. Presolve fixes the three variables and removes them (and the row), giving a smaller, tighter model.

source.label: Gurobi — "Mixed-Integer Programming (MIP): A Primer on the Basics" (archived copy on www-old.gurobi.com)

q: LP-based branch and bound for a minimisation MIP: when is a node fathomed, and what are the incumbent, the best bound and the gap?
a:
A node is fathomed when (i) its LP solution satisfies all integrality restrictions (it may become the new incumbent), (ii) its LP is infeasible, or (iii) its LP value is no better than the incumbent's value.
Incumbent value = upper bound. Best bound = minimum LP value over the current leaf nodes = lower bound. Gap = difference between the two; optimality is proven when the gap is zero.
Branching: pick an integer variable with a fractional LP value, e.g. $x=5.7$, and create the subproblems $x\le 5$ and $x\ge 6$. Good incumbents found early by heuristics allow more nodes to be fathomed.

q: Knapsack constraint $6x_1+5x_2+7x_3+4x_4+5x_5\le 15$ with binary variables. A fractional point has $x_3=x_4=x_5=3/4$. Which inequality is a valid cover inequality for the knapsack set and is violated by this point?
explain: $7+4+5=16 \gt 15$, so items 3, 4, 5 form a cover and cannot all be chosen: $x_3+x_4+x_5\le 2$ is valid; the point gives $9/4 \gt 2$ and is cut off. $\{1,2,4\}$ (weight 15) and $\{2,4,5\}$ (weight 14) are not covers, so their inequalities are invalid; $x_3+x_4+x_5\le 1$ is invalid because any two of these items fit.
